analysis.one_liner: Taxes opioid painkiller makers one cent per milligram to fund addiction treatment programs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from its May 2021 introduction until Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have charged manufacturers and importers of opioid painkillers a fee of one cent for every milligram of active opioid they sell. The money would have gone directly to states to fund addiction treatment — new treatment facilities, recovery housing, care for babies born in withdrawal, and hiring treatment providers in rural and underserved areas. The bill included protections for patients who legitimately need opioids, requiring rebates or discounts so cancer and hospice patients would not pay anything extra because of the fee.
analysis.who_benefits: People with opioid addiction and their families would gain access to more treatment programs, longer residential care, recovery housing, and provider recruitment in underserved areas, all paid for by the opioid fee. Cancer patients, hospice patients, and others whose doctors determine opioids are medically necessary would be protected from any cost increase through rebates or discounts. Communities hit hardest by the overdose crisis, especially rural ones, would see new treatment capacity.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with opioid addiction and their families

how_it_helps.text: Dedicates every dollar raised by the opioid fee, after patient rebates, exclusively to state substance abuse treatment programs, including new residential and outpatient facilities, sober living homes, and long-term 30-, 60-, and 90-day treatment programs [S3].

Funds recovery support services — employment help, housing, care for children whose parents are in treatment, and facilities for babies born with neonatal abstinence syndrome — plus recruitment of treatment providers in rural and medically underserved communities [S3].

Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to set up a rebate or discount mechanism so that eligible patients — cancer patients, hospice patients, and patients whose doctors determine other pain treatments are inadequate — face no economic burden from the fee [S3].

Directs HHS to report within two years on the fee's effect on retail opioid prices, patient access for cancer and hospice patients, and how the revenue is being used, so Congress would have to revisit the design if it harmed legitimate patients [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, producers, and importers of opioid painkillers bear the fee, one cent per milligram of active opioid sold. Some of that cost could be passed into retail prices for patients outside the protected categories, which is exactly why the bill built in rebates for cancer and hospice patients and required a report on retail price effects.

drawbacks.text: A per-milligram fee could raise retail prices for opioids, and legitimate pain patients who fall outside the bill's rebate categories — for example, some chronic-pain patients whose doctors consider opioids appropriate — could end up paying part of the fee at the pharmacy [S3].

The rebate mechanism depends entirely on HHS building it well: the fee would not even take effect until the Secretary established the rebate system, and the bill required a report on whether access for cancer and hospice patients actually held up [S3].
Tying ongoing treatment funding to a per-unit tax creates revenue that falls if opioid prescribing keeps declining, which could leave treatment programs funded on a shrinking base.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is substantial: dedicated, recurring funding for the treatment programs that communities hit by the overdose crisis repeatedly lack, financed by the companies that produce the opioids. The main risk is price pass-through to legitimate pain patients, which the bill tried to head off with rebates and a required access report. The design is cautious — the tax cannot even start until the patient-protection mechanism exists — but the rebate system's success would have depended on HHS implementation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Joe Manchin introduced the bill on May 20, 2021, with ten cosponsors including one Republican, Senator Mitt Romney [S3] [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; the committee took no further action [S5].
No vote was ever held in the Finance Committee or on the Senate floor, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers and importers are better off, since they never faced the per-milligram fee. States would not have received the dedicated treatment funding the bill would have directed to them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opioid manufacturers, who never paid the fee

against.name: Senate Republican leadership

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided — 8 of 48 Senate Democrats, 1 of 50 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 2 Independents signed on — and the bill never reached a vote, so there is no record of how the full chamber would have split.

industries.note: The fee of one cent per milligram on every active opioid sold would come directly out of their revenue. The industry's interest in the bill ran against ordinary people, since avoiding the fee meant treatment programs went unfunded; the bill's patient rebates show lawmakers expected the cost to be passed to consumers otherwise.

Dedicated funding for new treatment facilities, residential programs, and provider recruitment in underserved areas would have expanded their work and their workforce, in service of treating more people.
